::: {.section-card}
### Skills Mismatch

**What we compare**

- **Demand side** — every ESCO skill mention extracted from Pracuj.pl 2025 postings → **5.36 M mentions** across **~731k offers**
- **Supply side** — every BUR training service mapped to ESCO via semantic matching → **719,265 trainings**, **410,868 (training, ESCO-skill) tags**

**How we measure mismatch**

Both sides share the **same ESCO concept hierarchy** (L1: 25 main groups · L2: 205 sub-groups). For each group *g*:

- `demand_share[g] = mentions[g] / Σ mentions`
- `supply_share[g] = training_tags[g] / Σ training_tags`
- `gap_pp[g] = (demand_share − supply_share) × 100` (percentage points)

**How to read the result**

- **Gap > 0** → *under-supplied*: employers request the skill more often than the training system delivers it
- **Gap < 0** → *over-supplied*: training output exceeds the demand signal from online vacancies

**Why shares, not counts**

Both sides are **multi-tag** (one offer can mention many skills; one training can teach many skills). Comparing tag shares is scale-free and robust to the absolute volume gap between online vacancies and subsidised training listings.

**Caveats**

Online vacancies under-represent **public-sector and manual occupations**, where BUR is most active — the measured over-supply for personal-care and protective-service skills is partly a demand-side blind spot. BUR captures only the **subsidised and registered** slice of training supply; commercial and in-house training is absent from the supply side. We test how much these and other measurement choices affect the results in the [diagnostic cards at the end of this section](#mismatch-sensitivity).
:::

::: {.section-card}

Before drilling into skill pillars, the aggregate picture shows where tag mass concentrates on each side. **ESCO skills (S1–S8)** dominate demand mentions; **knowledge concepts** and **transversal competences** are also substantial. On the supply side, the S-pillar still leads, but **knowledge** and **assisting & caring** skills weigh more heavily than in vacancies — the first sign of compositional mismatch.

Conversely, **Assisting & caring (S3)**, **Working with machinery (S8)** and **Services (10)** are the largest *over-supplied* groups — partly reflecting EU-funded reskilling priorities and partly online vacancies under-representing those occupations.

::: {.section-card}
### Transversal, knowledge and language competences

The S-pillar summary masks important gaps in **transversal** and **knowledge** domains. Employers overweight **social & communication (T4)** and **self-management (T3)** relative to BUR; training supply is thin on both. Among knowledge fields, **business & administration (04)** and **ICT (06)** are under-represented in training tags, while **services (10)** and **health & welfare (09)** are over-represented — mirroring the care and public-service bias of subsidised programmes.

**Languages** are shown on a renormalised within-pillar basis (top nine demand languages plus an “Other” bucket; Polish and generic L1 tags excluded), matching the standalone mismatch charts. English and German still dominate employer demand; training supply is spread across several languages rather than appearing only on the demand side at near-zero global shares.

::: {.section-card}
### Measuring overall mismatch: Jensen–Shannon divergence

Treating skill shares as probability distributions, we summarise overall compositional distance with the **Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD)**. Values lie in **[0, 1]** (base 2): 0 means identical mixes; values around **0.16** indicate a moderate L1 (S1–S8) mismatch; **~0.30** at L2 signals a substantial reallocation need within skill sub-groups.

```{=html}
<div class="jsd-formula-wrap">
  <img src="presentation/jsd_formula.png" alt="Jensen-Shannon divergence formula" class="jsd-formula-img" width="720"/>
</div>
<p class="notes source-note">JSD compares renormalised S-pillar distributions on the demand and supply sides. L1 JSD ≈ 0.16; L2 JSD ≈ 0.30 (2025, Pracuj.pl vs BUR).</p>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> The JSD indicator summarises the overall distance between demand and supply skill distributions. The reported values suggest moderate mismatch at the broad skill-pillar level and more substantial mismatch at the detailed sub-group level.</p>
```
:::

### Are the mismatch results stable? {#mismatch-sensitivity}

The figures above rest on two non-trivial modelling choices: **how each
posting and training is weighted into the aggregate shares**, and
**which slice of the labour market the Pracuj.pl sample actually
represents**. Before drawing policy conclusions we need to know whether
the headline gap survives plausible alternative choices. The two cards
below answer that question. They are not new results — they are stress
tests of the results above. Each one states *why we are worried*, *what
we compute*, and *what we conclude*.

::: {.section-card .diag-card .diag-sensitivity}
#### Sensitivity — does posting verbosity drive the picture?

<span class="diag-kicker">Why we worry</span>

A senior CTO posting can list 20 ESCO skill mentions; a 1-line
warehouse-worker posting can list 1. Under the headline weighting scheme
("**mention-mass**") that CTO posting carries 20× more weight in the
demand shares than the warehouse posting. If ICT and management-heavy
postings are systematically more verbose than care-work postings, the
white-collar deficit could be partly an artefact of *how many tags get
written into a job description*, not of how many jobs are open.

<span class="diag-kicker">What we compute</span>

We rebuild the demand- and supply-side share vectors under a second
weighting scheme — **per-posting** — where each posting (or each
training) contributes exactly one unit of weight, distributed evenly
across the skills it mentions:

- mention-mass (headline): $s_g^{MM} = \dfrac{\sum_i \mathrm{count}_i(g)}{\sum_i |S_i|}$
- per-posting (alternative): $s_g^{PP} = \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_i \dfrac{\mathrm{count}_i(g)}{|S_i|}$

Then we compare the two vectors on each side and — more importantly —
on the **gap** (demand − supply) that actually drives every chart above.

<span class="diag-kicker">What we find</span>

| Comparison | L1 distance | Cosine similarity | Max single-group shift |
|---|---|---|---|
| Demand: MM vs PP | 0.061 | 0.998 | 0.81 pp (ICT, code 06) |
| Supply: MM vs PP | 0.034 | 0.9996 | 0.52 pp (generic language placeholder) |

And on the gap vector itself (54 ESCO L1 groups):

- Pearson r between MM- and PP-derived gaps: **0.998**
- max |Δ gap_pp| across all groups: **0.81 pp**
- top-10 **under-supplied** groups: **10 / 10 overlap** between the two schemes
- top-10 **over-supplied** groups: **9 / 10 overlap**

::: {.diag-verdict}
**Verdict.** ICT-heavy postings *do* list more ESCO tags than the
average posting, so the per-posting scheme shaves ~0.8 pp off ICT's
demand share. But no top-ranked under-supplied group moves and no
single group's share shifts by more than ~1 pp. The headline narrative
— large positive gap on management (S4), positive gap on digital (S5)
and ICT knowledge (06), negative gap on assisting & caring (S3) and
working with machinery (S8) — holds verbatim. Verbosity is not
driving the picture. We keep mention-mass as the headline because it is
the standard ESCO accounting unit and is comparable to other published
ESCO mention-rate studies.
:::
:::

::: {.section-card .diag-card .diag-robustness}
#### Robustness — does the Pracuj.pl sectoral skew drive the picture?

<span class="diag-kicker">Why we worry</span>

Pracuj.pl is a private-sector online job board. Some sectors are heavily
over-represented relative to actual Polish employment — most strikingly
**Administrative and support services (NACE section N, which includes
temp-work and recruiting agencies): 24.4 % of postings vs 2.75 % of
employment**, because agencies re-post vacancies that ultimately belong
to other sectors. Conversely, **agriculture (A), mining (B), education
(P), human health (Q) and information & communication (J)** are markedly
under-represented in the OJP universe relative to LFS employment shares.
A substantial part of the apparent skill mismatch could be a story about
"who advertises on Pracuj" rather than "what Poland's labour market
demands".

<span class="diag-kicker">What we compute</span>

Standard post-stratification. For each NACE section *k* we calculate a
sectoral weight

$$
w_k \;=\; \frac{p_k^{\text{target}}}{p_k^{\text{pracuj}}}
$$

where $p_k^{\text{target}}$ is section *k*'s share of total Polish
employment (Eurostat LFS 2024, ages 15+, both sexes — the international
counterpart of the GUS BAEL/LFS series "Pracujący w gospodarce
narodowej wg sekcji PKD") and $p_k^{\text{pracuj}}$ is its share in our
Pracuj.pl analysis sample. Each posting in section *k* enters the
aggregation with weight $w_k$, and the demand-side ESCO L1 shares are
recomputed on the weighted sample. Weights range from
$w_N \approx 0.11$ (administrative & support, heavily downweighted) to
$w_B \approx 15.4$ (mining, heavily upweighted); the median section
keeps roughly its OJP weight.

<span class="diag-kicker">What we find</span>

This is the largest perturbation we apply to the demand vector:

| Comparison | Result |
|---|---|
| L1 distance (headline vs reweighted) | **0.173** |
| Cosine similarity | **0.988** |
| Largest single-group fall | **−2.10 pp** for ICT knowledge (06) |
| Second-largest fall | −1.88 pp for management (S4) |
| Largest single-group rise | +1.51 pp for working with machinery (S8) |

The biggest *losers* under reweighting are the white-collar / digital
groups disproportionately mentioned by recruiting-agency,
finance and real-estate postings. ICT knowledge (06) falls from
**4.1 %** to **2.0 %**, management (S4) from **17.5 %** to **15.6 %**,
business & administration (04) from **7.6 %** to **6.2 %**. The biggest
*winners* are primary- and education-heavy groups: machinery (S8) rises
from **3.6 %** to **5.1 %**, education knowledge (01) from **2.6 %** to
**3.7 %**, agriculture/forestry/fisheries knowledge (A1) from **5.9 %**
to **6.5 %**.

What about the mismatch — the demand-minus-supply gap that every figure
above visualises?

- Pearson r between headline and reweighted gap vectors: **0.985**
- max |Δ gap_pp| across all groups: **2.10 pp**
- top-10 **under-supplied** groups: **9 / 10 overlap**
- top-10 **over-supplied** groups: **9 / 10 overlap**

::: {.diag-verdict}
**Verdict.** The directional conclusions hold across the board: large
positive gap on management and business/administration; meaningful
positive gap on transversal social skills; large negative gap on
assisting & caring, machinery and services. The single substantive
change is **the digital-skills deficit (working with computers S5 +
ICT knowledge 06): its magnitude is roughly halved once Pracuj is
reweighted to Poland's actual sectoral employment mix**. That tells us
roughly half of the headline digital gap is a *true* economy-wide
demand-supply imbalance and roughly half is a *composition effect* of
Pracuj over-sampling digital-intensive sectors. Both halves are still
policy-relevant, but for different reasons — the first calls for
adjusting subsidised training, the second for reading OJP-based
digital-skill indicators with appropriate humility.
:::
:::
